description: Generics basics — writing one function that works for many types.

screens.body:
Here's a puzzle: write a function that returns the first item of an array. It should work for string arrays, number arrays, user arrays — any array.

Without generics you have two bad options: write the function three times (one per type), or type everything as any and lose all checking. Generics are the third option: one function, many types, full checking.

options: One function that stays type-safe for any type
A function that only works with numbers
check.question: What problem do generics solve?

screens.heading: The duplication problem
screens.keyPoint: Generics = one function, many types, still type-safe.

screens.body:
A generic uses a type parameter — usually called T — as a placeholder for "whatever type the caller uses." You declare it in angle brackets before the parameters.

When someone calls first(["a", "b"]), TypeScript figures out T = string and the return type becomes string automatically. Call it with numbers, T = number. One definition, infinite uses.

options: <T> — a placeholder for the caller's type
check.question: What does the <T> in function first<T> mean?

screens.heading: <T>: a placeholder for a type
screens.keyPoint: T stands in for the type; TypeScript fills it in per call.

screens.body:
Interfaces can be generic too. A Box<T> holds a value of type T — a Box<string> holds a string, a Box<number> holds a number.

This is exactly how built-in types work: Array<string> is just a generic interface you've been using all along. Promise<User>, Map<string, number> — generics everywhere.

check.question: A Box holding a string is written…

screens.heading: Generic interfaces
screens.keyPoint: Box<T> — and Array<string> was generic all along.

screens.body:
Sometimes T can't be literally anything — you need it to have a certain shape. A constraint with extends says "T must at least look like this."

Now TypeScript lets you use .length inside the function, because every allowed T is guaranteed to have it. Constraints narrow the placeholder just enough.

check.question: How do you require T to have a length property?

screens.heading: Constraints: narrowing the placeholder
screens.keyPoint: extends sets the minimum shape T must have.

screens.body:
You can use more than one placeholder: <K, V> is the classic pair, used by Map and plain key-value helpers.

The letters are convention, not magic: T for Type, K for Key, V for Value, E for Element. Descriptive names like <ItemType> are fine too — clarity beats tradition.

check.question: In Map<K, V>, K and V conventionally mean…

screens.heading: More than one placeholder
screens.keyPoint: <K, V> — K for Key, V for Value.

screens.heading: Generics in the wild: typed fetch
screens.body:
The most common generic you'll actually write: a fetch wrapper. fetchData<User>("/api/me") returns Promise<User> — the response comes back typed, no casting, autocomplete works on every property.

Libraries do this everywhere: axios.get<User>(), useState<User>(). Once you see <T>, read it as "fill in your type here."
screens.keyPoint: fetchData<User> — fill in your type, get typed data back.

screens.body:
Generics are a tool, not a goal. If a function only ever handles strings, type it with string — don't add <T> "just in case."

Reach for generics when you see the same logic repeated for different types, or when you're building reusable utilities (like first, Box, or a fetch wrapper). Duplication twice is a hint; three times is a generic.

options: When the same logic repeats across types
check.question: When should you reach for generics?

screens.heading: When NOT to use generics
screens.keyPoint: Same logic, different types → generic. Otherwise, keep it simple.
